opportunities.title: 24/7 intake and trade-triage agent for overflow and after-hours calls
opportunities.problem: Every inbound request has to pass through a person before a job exists. The online booking page is a Gravity Forms request form with a single service-type dropdown (Heating, Cooling, Plumbing, Electric, Garage Doors, Generators) and a message field, with no live availability, so each web lead becomes a callback. The same phone line must also triage six lines of business on first contact and cover a footprint of roughly 100 towns across eight counties, while the company advertises that it answers 7 days a week, 365 days a year with 24/7 emergency service and no answering service. That is a human-staffed always-on desk on top of a reactive emergency load.
evidence: Online scheduling is a request form with a service-type dropdown and message field, not a calendar with live availability, so every web lead needs a human callback to convert (https://www.arcticac.com/schedule-online/)
Company states callers are never routed to a generic answering service and that it is available 7 days a week, 365 days a year with 24/7 emergency service (https://www.arcticac.com/about/)

Scheduling form already collects consent for appointment/service texts, marketing texts and phone calls 'including AI-generated voice calls' - an unusual clause that signals existing appetite for AI-handled voice contact (https://www.arcticac.com/schedule-online/)
Booking dropdown spans six distinct lines of business, so intake staff triage HVAC vs plumbing vs electrical vs generators vs garage doors at first contact (https://www.arcticac.com/schedule-online/)
Service area list runs to roughly 100 towns across Monmouth, Middlesex, Mercer, Somerset, Union, Ocean, Hunterdon and Morris counties (https://www.arcticac.com/service-area/)

Working paper (NBER w31161, flagged 'peer-reviewed' in the industry brief - treated here as a working paper): a generative-AI conversational assistant raised issues resolved per hour by 14% across 5,179 customer-support agents, with a 34% gain for novice agents. Support desk, not HVAC - transfer is an inference (https://www.nber.org/papers/w31161)
opportunities.agent_design: A voice + web intake agent sitting in front of the existing phone line and the Gravity Forms queue. Triggers: inbound call, after-hours call, or new web form submission. The agent greets, captures address against the ~100-town service-area table, classifies the request by trade (HVAC / plumbing / electrical / generator / garage door) and by urgency (no-heat/no-cool emergency vs routine), collects equipment and symptom details, then either books a slot against the dispatch calendar or creates a triage ticket with a summary and priority. Systems touched: phone/telephony (or SIP trunk in front of the existing number), the form endpoint, the dispatch/field-service calendar, and SMS for confirmation. Human approval points: any job above a configurable dollar or complexity threshold, any warranty or commercial account, any caller who asks for a person, and a same-day review queue of low-confidence classifications. After-hours behaviour is to book the next business slot or page the on-call tech per existing rules, never to quote price.
opportunities.why_not_DIY: A chatbot subscription cannot answer a phone, cannot see the dispatch calendar, and cannot decide whether a no-cool call in August is an emergency. This needs telephony integration, a trade-specific triage policy, a service-area/zone lookup, write access to the scheduling system, and an escalation path to a human within seconds. It also touches call recordings and home addresses, which the industry brief flags as a privacy-sensitive data class (PCI DSS, call-recording consent), so retention must be scoped and preferably vendor-private rather than a consumer chat widget.

impact_estimate.range: $60,000-$125,000/yr of front-desk capacity, plus recovered after-hours jobs (volume unknown until measured)
impact_estimate.assumptions: Assume a 3-6 person CSR/dispatch desk absorbing the phone and web queue. Median NJ customer service representative is $47,740/yr (https://api.bls.gov/publicAPI/v1/timeseries/data/OEUS340000000000043405113) and median NJ dispatcher $54,590/yr (https://api.bls.gov/publicAPI/v1/timeseries/data/OEUS340000000000043503213); fully loaded at ~1.3x that is roughly $62,000-$71,000 per FTE. If the agent reliably handles 45-70% of routine scheduling and status calls (inference from the 14% productivity figure in the NBER working paper, which measured assisted agents rather than deflection), that is 1.0-1.75 FTE-equivalents, or $62K-$124K. Deliberately excluded: revenue from recovered after-hours jobs, because Arctic Air publishes no average ticket - the pilot must measure it before any revenue claim is made.

opportunities.pilot_scope: 2-4 weeks: after-hours and overflow only (nights, weekends, and calls that ring out for more than N seconds). Deliverables: phone number or SIP forward, trade/urgency triage policy built with the service manager, live read/write to the dispatch calendar, SMS confirmation, a daily transcript-and-exception review queue, and a measured scorecard (calls handled, correctly triaged, booked vs callback, escalations, abandoned calls before vs after).

opportunities.title: Scheduling and dispatch coordination agent across 100 towns and the Comfort Club base
opportunities.problem: Scheduling is the load-bearing manual task in this business. Booking is form-to-callback, the recurring Comfort Club base adds a seasonal wave of 22-point tune-ups on top of reactive emergency calls, and membership sign-up and renewal run through a web form with no member self-service. Dispatch must match the right trade and skill to a wide radius and to a 16,000 sq ft parts warehouse stocked specifically so techs can finish in one visit - which only pays off if the right truck with the right part goes to the right town.
evidence: Online booking has no real-time availability, so every web request waits for a human callback before it becomes a scheduled slot (https://www.arcticac.com/schedule-online/)

Comfort Club maintenance membership includes a 22-point inspection, priority service and multi-year warranties, creating a recurring seasonal base of scheduled tune-ups on top of reactive calls (https://www.arcticac.com/comfort-club/)
Membership sign-up is an online form with 'call for full details and terms'; no member self-service portal is referenced anywhere on the site (https://www.arcticac.com/comfort-club/)
Service footprint of roughly 100 towns across eight counties plus separate commercial work sets a wide dispatch radius (https://www.arcticac.com/service-area/)
Large on-hand parts inventory is positioned as enabling same-visit repairs, which puts pressure on procurement and warehouse coordination (https://www.arcticac.com/contact/)

Preprint (arXiv 2211.16968, not peer-reviewed - labelled 'peer-reviewed' in the industry brief): a routing/scheduling optimisation tool cut travel time by about 16% on one telecom field-service instance; single-company evaluation, not residential HVAC (https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.16968)
opportunities.agent_design: Two linked agents. (1) A booking agent that replaces the form-to-callback loop: reads availability from the dispatch system, proposes 2-3 real slots that respect trade, technician skill/certification, zone and existing route, and confirms by SMS. (2) A seasonal coordination agent that reads the Comfort Club roster and service history, generates the tune-up plan by town cluster and month, sends the reminder/booking sequence under the existing SMS consent, and hands exceptions (lapsed members, warranty terms, commercial accounts) to a human. Systems touched: field-service/dispatch calendar, customer and membership records, SMS, parts/warehouse availability view. Human approval: dispatcher approves any re-route that moves another customer, all commercial jobs, all pricing, and any membership exception or discount.
opportunities.why_not_DIY: Requires write access to the dispatch system and a real model of technician skills, zones and travel time; a chat assistant cannot decide that a Trenton-bound truck can absorb a Monroe call at 2pm. The vendor ROI claims for field-service platforms (ServiceTitan's homepage promises higher profit and margins but publishes no auditable before/after metrics) give no number to buy against, so value has to be engineered against this company's own routes. Mis-scheduling also carries warranty and priority-service obligations from the Comfort Club terms.

impact_estimate.range: $40,000-$95,000/yr in recovered billable technician capacity, plus improved Comfort Club renewal capture
impact_estimate.assumptions: Assume 12-20 field technicians. NJ metro HVAC median is $77,990/yr (https://api.bls.gov/publicAPI/v1/timeseries/data/OEUM003562000000049902113), roughly $37-40/hr, so a recovered billable hour is worth about $37-40 in labor cost and more than that in margin. A 3-6% reduction in windshield/idle time on a 12-20 tech fleet equals about 0.4-1.2 tech-days per day, or $40K-$95K/yr at cost. The 16% travel-time figure in the arXiv preprint is NOT used directly - it is a single telecom instance and a preprint. Renewal uplift is left unquantified because no Comfort Club price or member count is published.

opportunities.pilot_scope: 2-4 weeks scoped to one trade and one zone: live-slot booking for routine cooling/plumbing calls in a subset of towns, plus the autumn/winter Comfort Club tune-up wave for one county. Deliverables: zone/skill/travel model, live-availability booking widget behind the existing form, reminder-and-rebook sequence for lapsed members, dispatcher approval console, and a before/after measure of travel minutes per job and booked-to-completed rate.

opportunities.title: Field and office knowledge agent built on Arctic Air University, warranty terms and refrigerant rules
opportunities.problem: Arctic Air runs mandatory in-house training ('Arctic Air University') with a full-time technical training manager, hires paid apprentices across HVAC, plumbing and electrical, and publishes an educational video series. That knowledge currently lives in people, documents and videos rather than in something a new tech can query at 9pm on a call. Meanwhile every job record it produces feeds manufacturer warranties and federally regulated refrigerant handling (EPA Section 608 certification and recordkeeping), so wrong or vague write-ups create warranty and legal exposure.
evidence: Arctic Air University is described as mandatory training for all new hires, run by a full-time technical training manager (https://www.arcticac.com/about/team/)
Careers page advertises fully paid apprenticeships in HVAC, plumbing and electrical, i.e. a continuous entry-level pipeline (https://www.arcticac.com/careers/)

Company produces a long-running blog and an educational YouTube series by its technical training manager - substantial existing written/video knowledge assets to index (https://www.arcticac.com/blog/)

Department managers are named for service, installation, plumbing/electrical, warehouse, sales and technical training, giving clear owners for a knowledge corpus (https://www.arcticac.com/about/team/)

Industry constraint: EPA Clean Air Act Section 608 requires technician certification and recordkeeping/reporting duties, so AI-generated refrigerant records create legal exposure (industry.json constraints; the EPA page was not opened in this pass, so this is cited from the brief rather than primary-sourced)

Industry constraint: job records feed OSHA-style safety compliance, manufacturer warranties and insurance claims, so AI-authored notes must be auditable and attributable to a technician (industry.json constraints)
opportunities.agent_design: A retrieval agent over the company's own corpus - Arctic Air University materials, manufacturer install/service manuals and fault-code references, Comfort Club terms and warranty language, and internal SOPs - answering in plain language with a citation to the source page or video timestamp. Two surfaces: a technician mobile/chat surface ('no heat, code E4, 80% furnace, what next') and an office surface for CSR questions about coverage, warranty and membership terms. A second, tightly bounded function drafts job-note summaries from technician voice memos for the tech to edit and sign. Systems touched: document store, video transcripts, job-note field in the field-service system. Human approval: every job note and any refrigerant record is technician-signed before it is saved; the agent never issues a compliance determination and defers code questions to a licensed interpretation.
opportunities.why_not_DIY: Needs a permissioned index of proprietary training material, manuals and warranty documents, plus write-back into the job record with an audit trail. Consumer chatbots either cannot see that corpus or would ingest customer and equipment data into a public model. The Section 608 and warranty exposure noted in the industry brief means the design must keep the human signature in the loop, which off-the-shelf assistants do not enforce.

impact_estimate.range: $15,000-$45,000/yr in reduced senior-tech hand-holding and faster apprentice ramp, plus fewer warranty/callback disputes (unquantified)
impact_estimate.assumptions: Assume 6-12 apprentices/new hires per year, each currently consuming 20-40 hours of senior-technician or training-manager time in the first months that a queryable corpus could cut by roughly a third. At a NJ HVAC median of $74,450 (about $36/hr, https://api.bls.gov/publicAPI/v1/timeseries/data/OEUS340000000000049902113) and a supervisor median of $105,510, saving 60-140 senior hours/yr lands at roughly $4K-$12K of direct labor, so the range is modest on labor alone. The larger, unquantified value is avoided callbacks and warranty disputes and reduced load on one training manager - deliberately not priced because Arctic Air publishes no callback or claim rates.

opportunities.pilot_scope: 2-4 weeks: index the existing training library and the top 20 equipment manual sets for one trade (HVAC), ship a technician-facing Q&A surface with source citations, and a voice-memo-to-draft-job-note flow with mandatory technician sign-off. Success measures: questions answered without phoning a senior tech, note-draft acceptance/edit rate, and time-to-first-independent-job for the current apprentice cohort.

lead_score.rationale: Pain (22/30): the friction is documented on Arctic Air's own pages - form-only booking, a human-staffed 24/7 promise, six trades on one intake form and roughly 100 towns - and the scheduling form already asks customers to consent to AI-generated voice calls, which is rare and specific. Held below the high 20s because no independent reviews could be retrieved, the field-service platform is unidentified, and no complaint or callback data exists to size the problem from the customer side. Fit (16/20): opportunities 1 and 2 are capability A on top of an existing phone line and dispatch system, and opportunity 3 is a clean C with a named training owner; E (warehouse sensors) was considered given the 16,000 sq ft parts facility but rests on a single sentence, so it is a later expansion, not a first sale. Ability to pay (15/20): roughly 80 staff and ~$19.4M revenue per unverified mapper sources, plus TurnPoint backing with 60+ brands and 180+ locations - real budget, but purchasing may sit at corporate rather than in Old Bridge. Ease (9/15): the technical pilot is straightforward, but no owner, president or GM is published, decisions are likely shared with TurnPoint corporate, and the dispatch platform is unknown, so early weeks are as much about finding the economic buyer as building. Strategic (14/15): a multi-trade contractor with a national parent is the most repeatable profile in this segment - one working intake-and-dispatch agent templates across TurnPoint's other brands. Total 76: strong prospect, qualified down by an opaque buying centre and thin third-party validation.

best_evidence_signal: The scheduling form already collects consent to be contacted by phone 'including AI-generated voice calls' - a clause most contractors do not carry, and direct evidence of appetite for AI-handled intake (https://www.arcticac.com/schedule-online/)
